items.title: Most of Britain was under ice 20,000 years ago
items.claim: How much of the UK was covered by ice at the Last Glacial Maximum?

options.text: None — Britain has never been glaciated
Most of the country north of the Thames was under ice up to around 1 km thick at the LGM (around 20,000 years ago), with southern England as a permafrost tundra zone
Only the Scottish Highlands were glaciated
All of the UK was under permanent ice until 1500 CE

items.reveal:
The British-Irish Ice Sheet extended to roughly the Thames-Severn line. Ice was up to 1 km thick over the Highlands. Glacial landforms — corries (Snowdonia, Lake District), U-shaped valleys (Glencoe), drumlins (Eden Valley) and erratics (Norber, Yorkshire) — record the maximum.

The Younger Dryas (around 12,900-11,700 years ago) was a final cold snap with small Highland glaciers (the Loch Lomond Stadial). Britain became ice-free by around 10,000 years ago.

Britain rejoined Europe geographically about 8,200 years ago when the Storegga submarine landslide tsunami finished off Doggerland.
items.why: Most British landforms are products of the Ice Ages, not earlier processes. The shape of the country is recent and contingent.

items.title: Scotland is still rising — England is sinking
items.claim: What is happening to the British Isles vertically due to glacial isostatic adjustment?

options.text: Both are stable — Britain has fully recovered from the last Ice Age
Scotland and northern England rise by 1-2 mm/year as crust rebounds from glacial loading; southern and eastern England sink by around 1 mm/year
All of Britain is sinking equally
The British Isles tilt is not measurable

items.reveal:
When the last ice sheet melted (about 10,000 years ago), the depressed crust began to rise. The mantle's slow viscous flow means rebound is still happening. GPS networks (BIGF, the British Isles GNSS Facilities) measure the motion directly.

Net result for relative sea level: southern England experiences faster sea-level rise than would be expected from climate alone, while northern Scotland experiences slower (or even falling) relative sea level. This is one reason why Thames and Hull tidal defences face accelerating pressure.

Fenno-Scandinavia is rising even faster (10 mm/year in parts of the Gulf of Bothnia).
items.why: Climate-change sea-level projections must be combined with local geophysics. A coast is rising or sinking on its own terms, and the climate signal sits on top of that.

items.title: The UK was under 1 km of ice at the Last Glacial Maximum
items.claim: How extensively was Britain glaciated around 20,000 years ago?

options.text: Only the Scottish Highlands had ice
The British-Irish Ice Sheet covered most of the country north of the Thames-Severn line, with ice up to 1 km thick over the Highlands; southern England was a permafrost tundra
All of Britain was permanently glaciated until 1500

items.reveal:
The LGM (around 20,000 years ago) saw the British-Irish Ice Sheet extending to roughly the Thames-Severn line. Ice thickness over the Highlands exceeded 1 km. Glacial landforms record the maximum: corries (Snowdonia, Lake District), U-shaped valleys (Glencoe), drumlins (Eden Valley, Ribblesdale), erratics (the Norber erratics, Yorkshire).

The Younger Dryas (around 12,900-11,700 BP) was a final cold snap — the Loch Lomond Stadial — producing small Highland glaciers and ice caps. Britain was largely ice-free by around 10,000 years ago.

Britain rejoined Europe by land until the Storegga submarine landslide tsunami around 8,200 years ago finally severed Doggerland.
items.why: Most British landforms are products of the Quaternary Ice Ages, not earlier processes. The country's shape and soils are recent, contingent and shaped by ice.
